prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The redbreast symbolizes a violent, self-destructive love that wounds itself while demanding to be remembered.
- The speaker is blinded and overwhelmed by this love, experiencing grotesque visions of drowning, vomiting, blood, feathers, and pain.
- The redbreast transforms suffering into something deceptively beautiful by wrapping injury in “pretty pink gauze” and presenting pain as desire.
- The bird inhabits the speaker’s mind, obsessively cleaning and scouring it until the inner world is stained red.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The, Sometimes, God

outputs.L1:
The redbreast kills and kills itself against the window.  
Sooner or later, the blood in its breast will break the window  
into hundreds of pieces you can swallow whole.

Keep swallowing.

The redbreast loves you and wants you  
to remember the love,  
so it makes you puke blindly into the toilet.

I was blinded by love  
and drowned in an empty bathtub,  
spitting up birdshit,  
covered in red feathers.

•

Sometimes the redbreast likes anting  
with lit cigarettes, safety pins, paper cuts.

God, that feels good.

It wraps everything in pretty pink gauze,  
the color of a fake sunset.

Look—it is a pink soul!

It wants to get naked,  
and it wants it to hurt.

Red teeth. Red toes.  
Open mouths.

Who keeps pressing  
my head into the sidewalk  
inside the bathroom?

Who keeps the lights on?  
The lights stay on.

Who dissolves on my tongue?  
Who flies from my finger?

•

The redbreast sits inside,  
behind your left eye,  
behind your right,  
and cleans its babies with its beak.

Scrubs its babies clean.

Shakes its tail feathers  
to scour the floor behind your forehead,  
and scours the floor red.

My brain is a cutter.  
My initials are beats per second,  
scrubbed down to zero  
by the rubies  
in the halo.

I whispered your name into the red air,  
and you answered.
outputs.L2:
Again and again, the robin hurls itself at the glass, killing and being killed. Eventually, the blood beneath its red chest will shatter the pane into hundreds of fragments, each small enough to gulp down. Do not stop swallowing.

The bird adores you. It needs you to retain proof of that devotion, so it leaves you sightless, vomiting into the toilet. Love took my vision. I sank in a bathtub with no water, coughing up bird filth, my body blanketed in crimson plumage.

At times, the robin practices anting with burning cigarettes, safety pins, and paper slices. God, the sensation is wonderful. It bandages everything in lovely rose-colored gauze, tinted like an artificial sundown. See—a soul in pink! It longs to strip bare, and it longs for pain.

Scarlet teeth. Scarlet toes.  
Mouths held open.

Who is forcing my skull against the pavement within the bathroom? Who refuses to turn off the lamps? The lamps never go dark. Who melts across my tongue? Who takes wing from the tip of my finger?

The robin makes its home inside you: behind the left eye, behind the right. With its bill, it washes its young, rubbing them spotless. It flicks its tail feathers, sweeping the space beyond your forehead until that inner floor has been scrubbed red.

My mind cuts itself. My initials measure heartbeats each second. The rubies set into the halo have scoured me away to nothing.

Into the crimson air, I breathed your name.

You replied.
outputs.L3:
The redbreast symbolizes a violent and self-destructive form of love—one that inflicts wounds upon itself even as it demands recognition and remembrance. Under its influence, the speaker becomes blinded and overwhelmed, experiencing grotesque visions of drowning, vomiting, blood, feathers, and physical pain. These disturbing images reveal love not as a source of comfort, but as an invasive force that destabilizes both body and mind.

At the same time, the redbreast disguises suffering as beauty. By wrapping injury in “pretty pink gauze,” it aestheticizes violence and presents pain as something tender and desirable. This deceptive transformation makes the love especially dangerous: suffering becomes difficult to resist because it is clothed in delicacy and attraction.

The bird also takes up residence within the speaker’s mind. It obsessively cleans, scrapes, and scours the speaker’s inner world until everything is stained red, suggesting that its attempts at purification only produce further damage. The color red unites love, blood, desire, and violence, showing how completely the redbreast has reshaped the speaker’s consciousness. Yet the ending offers a fragile possibility of connection. Although the speaker has been diminished and wounded by this force, they still reach outward through the “red air”—and receive an answer. This response does not erase the suffering, but it suggests that even within a world saturated by pain, communication and recognition remain possible.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents love not as a source of comfort or fulfilment, but as an obsessive force that consumes the speaker from within. At the centre of its imagery is a redbreast whose presence is at once delicate and brutal. Traditionally associated with tenderness, vulnerability, and song, the bird becomes an agent of psychological and physical torment, battering against the speaker’s body and mind as though trapped inside them. This surreal image gives emotional pain a visceral form: longing becomes an internal wound, and the beloved’s presence is experienced as something alive, restless, and impossible to remove.

The redbreast also embodies the contradictions of obsessive attachment. It is intimate because it inhabits the speaker’s innermost self, yet violent because that closeness causes continual injury. Love therefore collapses the distinction between affection and harm. The speaker cannot preserve the connection without suffering, but neither can they free themselves from it. The repeated sense of impact and agitation suggests a mind caught in cycles of memory, desire, and self-punishment. What might ordinarily be understood as devotion is transformed into compulsion, while emotional dependence becomes a form of self-destruction.

Through its bodily imagery, the poem suggests that psychological pain cannot be contained within abstract thought. It enters the flesh, disturbs the heart, and threatens the boundaries of identity. The speaker’s sense of self is gradually erased by the intensity of the attachment, as though love has occupied the space where an independent identity once existed. Yet this erasure is never complete. Memory remains, marked by injury, and the speaker continues to be haunted by what has been lost.

Ultimately, the poem offers an unsettling vision of connection. Love may bring two people close, but that closeness can also invade, consume, and destroy. The redbreast’s fragile body preserves the possibility of tenderness, even as its frantic violence makes tenderness inseparable from suffering. What survives is not a stable relationship or a healed self, but a wound that still carries the memory of intimacy. In this way, the poem leaves open the haunting possibility that connection is both necessary and dangerous: the very force that allows one person to enter another’s inner world may also be the force that breaks it apart.
outputs.L5:
**The Silence of God**

Sometimes, God speaks through silence—not as an absence, but as an invitation to listen more deeply. In the quiet between questions and answers, we may discover courage, patience, or a path we had not noticed before. The difficulties of life do not always disappear through faith, yet faith can help us carry them. Sometimes, the smallest signs—a kind word, an unexpected sunrise, a hand offered in friendship—remind us that hope is still present.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem about a redbreast trapped inside the speaker’s body, using violent surreal imagery, fractured spacing, and themes of self-harm, obsessive love, and purification.
counterfactuals.output:
There is a redbreast trapped behind my ribs.

Not metaphor—  
not mercy—

a fist-sized furnace battering the white bars,  
beak bright with the alphabet of wounds.

Each morning it mistakes my heart for dawn  
and sings  
           sings  
                    until the mirrors blister.

I loved you obsessively: as salt loves an open mouth,  
as fire loves the house it enters. I kept your name  
under my tongue until it became a blade of light.  
When I spoke, everything tender split.

Inside me, the bird panics.

It hurls itself from lung to lung, leaving feathers  
in the weather of my blood. I press my palms  
against the cage of myself, wanting silence—  
wanting punishment—  
wanting your hand to arrive like a clean white cloth  
and call the damage holy.

But you are elsewhere, drinking from ordinary cups.

So I become the altar and the animal.  
I make small ceremonies of ruin:  
the closed door, the bitten lip, the thought sharpened  
and sharpened, though I swear I will not use it.  
My body wears the night like wet gauze.

       red     red  
              little engine of accusation

What must be broken to be pure?

The redbreast answers by tearing the dark  
into ribbons. Its wings beat soap from bone,  
snow from marrow. It wants to wash me  
in the violent basin of its breast.

I open my mouth.

A feather rises. Then another.

Not blood—  
berries.  
Not wounds—  
windows.

The bird climbs my throat, furious with morning,  
and for one impossible second I believe love  
is not the knife, nor the hand, nor the gleaming need—

but the cage unlatching.

Still, it does not leave.

It settles behind my teeth, trembling,  
and sings your name so softly

I survive it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a disturbing, stream-of-consciousness poem in which a robin repeatedly crashes into a window and becomes a metaphor for destructive love.
counterfactuals.output:
The robin keeps mistaking the window for mercy.

Again—  
red breast, small fist of weather,  
a bright blunt syllable against the glass.

And again.

I say stop, though I mean come back.  
I say love, though I mean  
leave your shape on me.

There is a tree reflected in the window  
that does not exist on this side,  
a blue country folded over the room,  
a counterfeit sky trembling  
above the sink.

The robin sees a world  
and hurls its whole red heart toward it.

Tap—  
then feather-scrabble,  
then the stunned little body  
collecting itself from the sill.

You loved me like that, didn’t you,  
believing the barrier was only distance,  
believing enough speed could turn refusal  
into an opening—

again—

the beak clicking glass  
like a tooth in a fever dream,  
the wings beating nowhere,  
the window giving nothing back  
but another robin,  
another wound-colored breast,  
another lover arriving at the same disaster.

I should close the curtain.

I should.

But the sound has entered me now,  
a clock made of bone,  
a knock from inside the house  
though I am inside the house,  
though you are gone,  
though gone is only another pane  
we fling ourselves against.

Again—

and there is blood, or sunset,  
or nothing, only that red  
the robin was born carrying,  
that flag of need,  
that tiny burning room.

It falls.

It rises.

It sees paradise exactly where paradise is not.

Darling, I know.

I know the false branches,  
the beautiful impossible depth,  
the cold invisible fact between wanting  
and being let through.

Still, when it strikes again,  
my heart answers—

not with pity,

but recognition.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an avant-garde horror poem centered on red feathers, blood, pink gauze, cigarettes, bathrooms, blindness, and a bird living behind the eyes.
counterfactuals.output:
**ORNITHOLOGY OF THE WOUND**

In the bathroom, the mirror practices blindness.  
It fogs at the edges,  
forgets the face first.

Red feathers clog the sink—  
small flames rinsed from an animal  
no one remembers killing.

I wrap my mouth in pink gauze.  
It blooms darkly where I breathe.  
Each word is born pre-bandaged.

On the toilet tank:  
three cigarettes, upright in a glass,  
their ash lengthening  
like the fingers of dead nurses.

Behind my eyes  
a bird has built its terrible room.

At night it turns around in me,  
scratching the sockets,  
dragging twigs through the blood.

I cannot see it.  
I see only what it sees:

a corridor feathered red,  
a bathtub full of whispering,  
the moon shaved down  
to a wet white razor.

Someone knocks from inside the mirror.

I answer by bleeding.

The pink gauze loosens.  
The cigarettes inhale themselves.  
Every bathroom stall swings open  
onto the same black sky.

Then the bird pecks once—

and blindness pours in,  
warm as bathwater.

By morning, my eyes are empty nests.  
On the tile, two red feathers  
lie crossed like evidence.

From somewhere behind them  
comes the soft, soft sound  
of wings  
learning my name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary free-verse poem with minimal punctuation and irregular line breaks. Include the refrain-like figure of “the redbreast,” visceral body imagery, and the line “My brain is a cutter.”
counterfactuals.output:
the redbreast arrives  
like a small wound  
learning to sing

morning has teeth  
in the sink  
my mouth tastes of iron

My brain is a cutter.

it trims the light  
into narrow strips  
slides each silver edge  
beneath the day

the redbreast  
on the fire escape

a thumbprint of blood  
with wings

inside me  
the heart keeps shouldering  
its wet door

the lungs bloom and collapse  
two bruised flowers  
refusing the vase

someone downstairs laughs  
a chair scrapes  
the city lifts its rib cage  
and coughs

the redbreast waits

bright pulse  
black eye

I offer it nothing  
but this body  
stitched from hunger  
and ordinary hours

still it sings

still the redbreast  
presses its fierce little flame  
against the glass
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal confessional piece about being consumed and cleansed by love, blending bird behavior such as anting and preening with images of broken glass, an empty bathtub, red air, and a glowing halo.
counterfactuals.output:
I confess: I mistook your hunger for mercy.

You opened your mouth and the room filled with red air. Curtains breathed it. The walls blushed through their plaster. Even the broken glass on the floor held small crimson suns in its teeth. I stepped toward you barefoot, believing every wound was another door.

You consumed me slowly, with the patience of weather. First my name, then the hands I had used to hide inside it. You swallowed my sleep, my old excuses, the little locked chapel behind my ribs. When you reached my heart, you did not bite. You held it on your tongue until it forgot which body had taught it to beat.

Afterward, I lay in the empty bathtub, clean of everything but longing. No water ran, yet I heard an ocean leaving me. Above the drain, a glowing halo hovered—crooked, electric, too bright to be holy. I wore it anyway.

I began anting like a wounded bird: gathering the sharp, medicinal creatures of memory and pressing them beneath my wings. Their small acids burned through grief’s parasites. I trembled with purification. I spread myself over the broken glass and let each shard become an ant, each ant a fever, each fever a prayer.

Then came the preening.

With my mouth, I arranged what remained of me. I smoothed the barbs of my feathers, drew each ruined filament back into its neighbor, and cleaned your shadow from the difficult places. I worked carefully around the scars. Love had eaten me, yes—but in being eaten, I had passed through the red furnace of you and emerged strange, hollow-boned, shining.

Now I perch on the bathtub’s porcelain edge, halo humming above my head. The red air thins toward morning. Beneath me, the drain keeps its black eye open.

I confess: I still call this cleansing.

I confess: when I lift my wings, I can smell you burning there.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
